cells.tense: Right now the threads are coming together, and the shape belongs to the group.
cells.act: act on the private sense of what is right
cells.ask: When a familiar custom crosses your day, notice whether it still fits. Let that quiet answer settle the small case before the loudest voice does.
cells.core:
You can tell when a custom still fits. People ask what is right in a disagreement and you feel it before you can argue it, and you say it, and the group moves. That sense is yours; nobody installed it.

It's also the thing most likely to be handed off to the group. The quiet knowing gets checked against the loudest voice, and the fair call arrives a minute late. So when some piece of the shared practice passes through your hands, let the private answer come first. No announcement, no ledger. Nobody tallies it, which is the whole point.
cells.sheetLine: Your sense of what is fair arrives before anyone asks.
cells.verb: gathering scattered threads of thought into a shape a group can carry

cells.tense: You're already writing next season's version of the tradition in your head.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Take the next piece of something the group needs — not all of it, just the piece you can carry — and move at a pace that part can keep.
cells.core:
By this point the gathering has a schedule, and the schedule is running past the people in it. You are holding several lines of thought at once and nobody else is holding them yet, so the pace you set is a pace they don't own. The group has become a project you are managing.

If you look, you can feel which part of this you actually want to move and which part is just pressure to arrive. Go at the pace that part can sustain. That's the way back here — a direction you can feel in your feet. The steady version loses the drama, and that's the trade.
cells.sheetLine: The next step moves faster than the people it belongs to.

cells.tense: You stopped gathering anything, and the old shapes hold their places without you.
cells.act: spend an hour with the thing you love without a task attached to it
cells.ask: Give an afternoon to one piece of the inherited practice you grew up with. No fixing, no explaining, no verdict — just the quiet of it.
cells.core:
The rituals went through you and you were elsewhere. You can still recite them; the words sit in memory, but nothing in you is collected around them, and nothing is being handed forward by your hand. The parts are all there and they haven't joined.

What holds goes deeper than opinion. There's something in you that already knows how this tradition has treated you, and that knowing doesn't need to be argued into shape. Give it time that asks nothing back. Not to heal the whole matter — you are not opening that today. You are sitting down with what your heart has been carrying in the next room.
cells.sheetLine: The old shapes hold their places. You are not in them.

cells.tense: The fire under the shared practice is yours and you call it the group's.
cells.act: share the joy with the people it belongs to
cells.ask: When something in the shared practice goes well, say so where the others can hear it — plain, glad, no report attached. Let them have the good news as it happens.
cells.core:
You've been tending the younger ones through this. Somebody brings you the question about the old form and you answer it; you say you're just one of the crowd. The knack for passing it on is the thing itself, and you have been describing it as attendance.

Follow what started it. When some piece of the practice lands — a thing you made, a thing you were part of — tell someone it delighted you, plain, without a report attached. Not to be thanked. It's the good news it is, and it's yours to hand over. That's what makes the tradition breathe instead of the group holding it up.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is collecting scattered thoughts into strategy while missing their living part in a shared tradition — Flocking's record says nothing about what they have built or joined, only how the capacity engages. A reader could reasonably say the tradition holds them and their own dislike of the reciting has nothing to do with what they wanted, though the cell assumes they wanted something when they took it on. The ask survives if the read is wrong: handing over one piece of their own keeps working regardless of why they carry the rest. The sentence that serves me rather than them is any line about what the tradition does to them — cut it; the person's hands are the subject.
